A checkpoint is a snapshot of my trained weights saved under _model_trained/. Ask me to 'checkpoint the model' or use the Model checkpoints card in the Mind tab, and you can load any snapshot back as my active brain.

pairs.q: how do i save your model
pairs.a: Say 'checkpoint the model' (or 'train and save the model' to train first). It lands in _model_trained/ with weights + metadata you can load or download later.

Cortex LLMHoster is a free local model hoster by codero-sus (github.com/codero-sus/Cortex_LLMHoster). It runs models on your machine with an OpenAI-compatible API, and I can route open questions to it — it serves models, while my own NumPy brain is what trains.
Ollama (ollama.com) is a popular local model runner. I can route open questions to any model you've pulled there — configure it in Mind → Local LLM · Ollama.

pairs.q: how do i change your model
pairs.a: Use the dropdown next to the send button: Auto, my self-trained brain, or a specific Cortex/Ollama model. In Auto mode I answer from my brain first and only route open questions to hosted models.

pairs.q: how do i export our chat
pairs.a: Press the ⬇️ export button in the chat status bar — you'll get the whole conversation as a Markdown transcript.

pairs.q: how do i run the self evaluation
pairs.a: Mind tab → 🧪 Self-eval. It tests my math, identity, knowledge and principles and shows per-question results.
The Growth tab shows my learning curve (loss after each training round), vitals like vocab size and feedback counts, Train now / Dream buttons, recent activity, and software updates.

The Mind tab shows my CORTEX self-learning loop: trainer status, self-eval, constitution principles, semantic facts, lessons, skills, goals, the Cortex and Ollama backend cards, model checkpoints and chat-history import.
The Learn tab is where you teach me question→answer pairs directly and browse everything I know so far.
My loss measures how surprised my language model is by the conversations it has seen. Training lowers it — the Growth tab charts every round.
Backpropagation computes how each weight contributed to the error, using the chain rule, so gradient descent knows which direction to nudge every weight.
Gradient descent repeatedly steps weights downhill against the loss gradient. I use Adam, a momentum-plus-adaptive-scale variant, for every training round.
Adam combines momentum with per-parameter adaptive learning rates — robust defaults, fast progress on small models like mine.
Tokenization splits text into the units a model reads. Mine is a simple lowercase word tokenizer shared by my memory and language model.
An embedding maps a word (or text) to a vector of numbers so that similar things end up close together in space. My input layer E is exactly that.

pairs.q: what is a large language model
pairs.a: An LLM is a neural network trained to predict the next token over huge corpora. I'm a tiny transparent cousin: same idea, NumPy-scale, trained on our conversation.
GPT means Generative Pre-trained Transformer — an autoregressive language model. My name nods to it, but I'm a small feedforward net that trains itself on what you teach me.
NumPy is Python's array math library. My entire brain — embeddings, hidden layer, softmax, Adam — runs on it, no GPU needed.
An API is a contract for talking to software. My Flask server exposes JSON endpoints like /api/chat and /api/stats that the WebUI calls.
HTTP is the request/response protocol of the web. This page, my stats, and the Cortex and Ollama backends all speak it.
JSON is a lightweight text format for structured data — my memory, metrics and checkpoints metadata are all JSON.

Growth tab → Software updates → Check for updates, then confirm the exact commit to install — or run ./updater.sh (updater.bat on Windows). Updates come from the pinned codero-sus/MyGPT branch and never touch your data/ folder.
The MyGPT Personal-Use License: free to download and run unmodified for personal, non-commercial use. Modification, redistribution and commercial use need written permission from codero-sus.
No — MyGPT is semi-closed source. Selling, sublicensing or commercial use requires written permission from codero-sus.
Under the personal-use license, no — you may run unmodified copies for personal, non-commercial use. Ask codero-sus for written permission for anything else.
On GitHub: github.com/codero-sus/MyGPT — and the author's profile github.com/codero-sus has the whole project family (agi/CORTEX, Cortex LLMHoster).
codero-sus is my author — GitHub: github.com/codero-sus, website: the-codero.web.app. Their projects include MyGPT, the CORTEX self-learning loop (agi) and Cortex LLMHoster.
Three ways: the Teach panel in the Learn tab, a 👎 with a correction on any answer, or just chatting — every turn trains me in the background.
Our conversation, corrections and taught pairs go into my corpus; Adam steps over it lower my loss. Rounds run automatically after enough feedback, or press Train now in the Growth tab.
My constitution is a list of durable principles distilled from self-critique lessons — like 'state what would falsify a claim'. See it in the Mind tab.
Skills are small Python files in skills/ that I write when one intent keeps repeating — procedural memory. The Mind tab lists them.
Episodic memory stores our actual turns with timestamps and embeddings, so I can recall similar past moments — that's what restores your chat after a page reload.
Dreaming samples fresh sentences from my language model, and my dream-replay text (principles + facts + dialogue) is re-learned by the idle trainer. Try 💭 Dream in the Growth tab.
No. I run entirely on your machine — Flask + NumPy. Optional Cortex/Ollama backends are local too, so prompts never leave your computer.
Markdown is a lightweight text format — **bold**, *italic*, # headings, `code`. My chat export downloads your conversation as Markdown.
Git is distributed version control — snapshots of a project you can diff, branch and roll back to. My updater installs confirmed commits of my own repo with it.
A database stores structured data for fast lookup. Mine is deliberately simple: JSON files in data/ for memory, corpus, metrics and episodes — inspectable and portable.
Stop the server and delete the data/ folder — I wake up with amnesia and my seed knowledge. Checkpoints in _model_trained/ are untouched, so you can reload an older brain.

pairs.q: how do i switch to light mode
pairs.a: Click the 🌓 button in the top bar. Your choice is remembered in localStorage, and on first visit I follow your system's prefers-color-scheme.

pairs.q: how do i search the chat
pairs.a: Type in the search box above the chat (or press Ctrl+K) — messages that don't match are hidden live. Escape clears the search.

pairs.q: how do i clear the chat
pairs.a: Click 🗑 clear in the model bar and confirm. It wipes the visible transcript and the saved copy — my learned memory is untouched.
Yes. POST /api/chat/stream returns Server-Sent Events and the WebUI types the answer in live, word by word. Plain /api/chat still works for scripts.

Enter send · Shift+Enter newline · Escape clear · / focus composer · Ctrl+K search · Alt+1/2/3 tabs · ↑ recall last message · Ctrl+Shift+E export · Ctrl+Shift+L clear chat · double-click a message to copy it.

pairs.q: how do i copy just the code
pairs.a: Every code block has a ⧉ button in its header bar — one click copies only the Python, not the surrounding text.
Colouring code by role — keywords, strings, comments, numbers. My chat colours Python blocks right in the browser with a tiny dependency-free highlighter.

pairs.q: how do i change the font size
pairs.a: Use the A− / A+ buttons in the top bar. The zoom level is saved, so it survives reloads.

pairs.q: how do i print the conversation
pairs.a: Just press Ctrl+P. A print stylesheet hides the sidebars and buttons so only the chat transcript goes to paper or PDF.

pairs.q: how do i import a chat file by drag and drop
pairs.a: Drag a .txt or .json chat export onto the chat panel — it highlights as a drop zone and imports on release, same as the file picker in the Mind tab.
A Progressive Web App — a website with a manifest and icons so browsers offer 'install to desktop/home screen'. MyGPT ships a manifest.json.
manifest.json tells the browser my name, icons, colours and start URL — that's what powers the install prompt. Fetch it at /manifest.json.
Both ways: '42 in roman' → XLII, and 'XIV in numbers' → 14. I validate spellings, so IIII is rejected but IV works.
Length (m, km, cm, mm, miles, inches, feet, yards), mass (kg, g, pounds, ounces) and temperature (°C ↔ °F). Ask like '5 km in miles' or '100 celsius in fahrenheit'.
Yes — '100 celsius in fahrenheit' → 212 °F and '32 f to c' → 0 °C. Just ask in plain words.
How much a value moved, relative to the start: (new − old) / |old| × 100. Ask me 'percent change from 50 to 75' → 50%.

pairs.q: can you average a list of numbers
pairs.a: Yes — 'average of 3, 5, 7' → 5. I also do sum, total, max and min of number lists, plus '20% off 100' and '15 is what percent of 60'.
GET /api/version returns my version plus codero-sus's GitHub and website links — handy for scripts and health dashboards.

pairs.q: what is the memory search endpoint
pairs.a: GET /api/memory/search?q=… returns my top matching Q→A pairs with weights — the raw retrieval layer behind chat, exposed for inspection.
GET /api/suggest?q=… autocompletes from everything I know — up to six question titles matching your fragment.
GET /api/backends/models lists every answerable engine in one call: my brain, plus all Cortex LLMHoster and Ollama models.
Yes — /robots.txt politely asks crawlers to stay off the JSON API. Small thing, but it's good web citizenship.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — HTTP headers that let other origins call an API. My /api/* routes send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * so local scripts and dashboards can use me.
SSE is one-way streaming over HTTP: the server pushes 'data:' lines as they're ready. My streaming chat endpoint uses it — simpler than WebSockets for token streams.

pairs.q: how many code templates do you have
pairs.a: Over eighty template families — from primes and fizzbuzz to hangman, decorators, dataclasses, scrapers and argparse CLIs. Ask for code and I'll show a block in chat.

pairs.q: how many tests do you have
pairs.a: Around ninety unittest cases in tests/ — tokenizer, memory, math, conversions, codegen, checkpoints, the API and the brain pipeline. Run them with python -m unittest discover -s tests.

pairs.q: how do i recall my last message
pairs.a: Press ↑ (ArrowUp) in an empty composer — your last sent message comes back for editing.

pairs.q: how do i switch tabs with the keyboard
pairs.a: Alt+1 opens Learn, Alt+2 Growth, Alt+3 Mind.

pairs.q: how do i focus the search box
pairs.a: Ctrl+K jumps to the chat search; Escape clears it. '/' still focuses the composer.

pairs.q: how do i export with a keyboard shortcut
pairs.a: Ctrl+Shift+E downloads the Markdown export; Ctrl+Shift+L clears the chat.
Yes — the layout is responsive, the composer grows with your text, and touch users get the same buttons. The sidebars stack under the chat on narrow screens.

pairs.q: how do i copy a whole message
pairs.a: Double-click any bubble to copy its text, or use the ⧉ button under bot replies.
4000 characters per message, mirrored by the composer's maxlength and enforced server-side with a 400. The counter appears once you pass 3000.

pairs.q: how do i teach many pairs at once
pairs.a: POST /api/teach/bulk with {"pairs": [{"question": …, "answer": …}, …]} — up to 100 per call. Each pair is validated and reported individually.
The three animated dots while I think — they're replaced by the streamed reply as words arrive.
A subtle 'Today' line between messages from different days, so long transcripts stay oriented in time.
Yes — Python code blocks get keywords, strings, comments, numbers and decorators coloured, computed in-browser with no external library.

pairs.q: what is a decorator in python
pairs.a: A function that wraps another to add behaviour — @timed, @staticmethod, @app.get. Ask me for 'decorator example code' and I'll show a timing decorator.

pairs.q: what is a generator in python
pairs.a: A function using yield — it pauses and resumes, producing values lazily instead of building a whole list. Ask for 'generator example code'.
A chain of nodes where each stores a value and a pointer to the next. Insert/delete is O(1) at a known node, lookup is O(n).
Last-in-first-out: push adds to the top, pop removes it — like a stack of plates. Ask for 'stack and queue code'.
First-in-first-out: enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front — like a checkout line.
A structure mapping keys to values via a hash function, giving average O(1) lookup. Python's dict is one.
A tree where each node has at most two children. Search trees keep left < node < right for fast lookup.
A tree where the smallest (min-heap) or largest (max-heap) item sits at the root — Python's heapq is a min-heap.
A set of nodes joined by edges, directed or not, weighted or not. BFS and DFS are the basic traversals.
Exploring a graph level by level with a queue; finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
Diving as deep as possible before backtracking, usually with recursion or an explicit stack.
How cost grows with input size: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²). It's the shape of the curve that matters.
A sort that keeps equal items in their original order — Python's sorted() is stable.
A function calling itself on a smaller subproblem with a base case that stops it. Never forget the base case.
Combining solutions to overlapping subproblems and storing them so no work repeats — memoisation or bottom-up tables.
Taking the locally best choice each step, hoping for a global optimum. Fast, but only correct for some problems.
Keeping a moving range over a list to avoid rescanning — O(n) instead of O(n²) for subarray problems.
Walking two indices through a sorted list (from both ends or offset) to find pairs or ranges in linear time.
Caching a function's results so repeat calls are instant — functools.lru_cache does it in one line.
A double-ended queue from collections with O(1) append/pop at both ends — great for stacks and queues alike.
A function using yield to produce values lazily, one at a time, instead of materialising a whole list.
An object usable with 'with' that sets up and tears down a resource via __enter__/__exit__ or @contextmanager.
A nested function that remembers variables from the enclosing scope even after that scope returned.
Python checks behaviour, not declared types — anything with the right methods works.
The Global Interpreter Lock: one thread runs Python bytecode at a time. Use processes or native code for CPU-bound parallelism.
Optional annotations like def f(x: int) -> str that document types and let mypy/pyright verify them statically.
A third-party test runner using plain asserts and fixtures. MyGPT's suite uses stdlib unittest so no extra dependency is needed.
An isolated folder with its own interpreter and packages so project versions never clash: python -m venv .venv.
Python's style guide: 4-space indents, snake_case functions, CapWords classes, 79 columns as a soft rule.
A prebuilt package archive (.whl) that pip installs without compiling — faster and more reliable.
A file listing dependencies so 'pip install -r requirements.txt' recreates the environment.
The first line like #!/usr/bin/env python3 telling the OS which interpreter to run the script with.
It checks whether the file is run directly rather than imported — guarded code only executes as a script.
The reach of a name: local → enclosing → global → builtin (LEGB). global and nonlocal rebind outer names.
Objects that can't change after creation — ints, strings, tuples. Their immutability makes them safely shareable and hashable.
Assigning several names at once: a, b = b, a swaps; first, *rest = items grabs a head and the remainder.
An immutable set — hashable, so it can be a dict key or sit inside another set.
bytes hold raw 8-bit data, str holds unicode text. Encode to go text → bytes, decode to return.
A string prefixed with r where backslashes stay literal — essential for regexes and Windows paths.
Building strings with f-strings (f'{name}: {score:.1f}'), .format() or % — f-strings are the modern default.
The string method that glues an iterable together: ', '.join(words) beats repeated + in a loop.
':=' assigns inside an expression: while (line := f.readline()): — Python 3.8 and newer.
An inline if/else: 'pass' if score >= 50 else 'fail'.
Structural pattern matching (3.10+): match command: case ['go', direction]: ...
Use 'raise NewError(...) from original' to keep the original cause attached instead of hiding it.
Code that runs no matter what — success, exception or return. Perfect for closing files and connections.
A class inheriting from Exception that names a specific failure, e.g. class QuotaExceeded(Exception).
DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL; a handler emits messages at or above its level.
A thread that dies with the main program — thread.daemon = True keeps shutdown clean.
Two threads touching shared state in an unexpected order. Fix with a lock, a queue, or by avoiding shared state.
Cooperative concurrency: async functions pause at await so thousands of I/O operations overlap on one thread.
The object returned by calling an async function — it must be awaited or scheduled on an event loop.
The scheduler running coroutines, resuming them when awaited I/O is ready. asyncio provides Python's.

pairs.q: what is the difference between process and thread
pairs.a: Processes have separate memory (true parallelism, heavier); threads share memory (cheaper, GIL-limited for CPU work).
Spawning real OS processes to bypass the GIL for CPU-bound work, with queues and pools to collect results.

pairs.q: what is a memory leak in python
pairs.a: Usually an unintended reference — a growing cache, global list or closure — keeping objects alive. tracemalloc finds it.
Python frees objects when their reference count hits zero, plus a cycle collector for reference loops.
A tool flagging style and bug risks without running code — flake8, ruff and pylint are common.
A tool that rewrites code to a canonical style; black and ruff format are the popular choices.
Static verification of your annotations: mypy and pyright are the best known.
Continuous Integration: a service that runs your tests on every push — GitHub Actions is free for public repos.

pairs.q: what is a pre commit hook
pairs.a: A script run before each commit (see the pre-commit framework) to lint, format or test automatically.
Recording exact versions (package==1.2.3) so today's working install reproduces tomorrow.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking changes bump major, features minor, fixes patch. MyGPT follows it.
A human-readable list of notable changes per release — this project keeps every improvement numbered in CHANGELOG.md.
Previously working behaviour that broke. Tests are how you catch them; a failing test is a gift, not an obstacle.
The share of lines a suite executes — useful as a map of untested areas, misleading as a quality score.
Replacing a real dependency with a fake in tests — like pointing the Cortex client at a dead port to prove offline behaviour.
Reusable test setup: a temp directory, a seeded brain, a fake server.
Describe rules and let a tool (hypothesis) generate hundreds of random inputs trying to falsify them.
Keeping old clients working as the interface evolves — new paths, new fields, never silent breakage.
A tiny endpoint (/api/health here) reporting whether a service lives and its dependencies answer.
A component spreading traffic across instances so no single server is overwhelmed.
Edge servers that serve static files near the user, cutting latency and origin load.
I'm a teapot — an April Fools' RFC joke that survived in real libraries. I stick to honest status codes.
An operation giving the same result however many times it runs — GET and PUT should be idempotent, POST need not.
A persistent two-way connection over an HTTP upgrade; great for chat. My streaming uses simpler one-way server-sent events.
Repeating requests the server holds open until data exists — the pre-SSE way to fake push.
A JSON document describing the shape of other JSON documents, used to validate requests and generate docs.
A standard way to describe HTTP APIs; from it you can generate docs, clients and tests.
Content-Security-Policy: headers restricting which scripts and frames a page may load. The Cortex dashboard sets a strict one.
Cross-site scripting: injecting script into a page. Prevent it by escaping user text — chat here uses textContent, never innerHTML.
SQL injection: unescaped input altering a query. Always use parameter placeholders (?), never string formatting.
Cross-site request forgery: another site posting as you. Defences include SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens.
Random data added before hashing so identical passwords give different digests, defeating rainbow tables.
Hashing is one-way (verify, never recover); encryption is reversible with a key (protect, then decrypt).
Comparing secrets without leaking timing information — hmac.compare_digest does exactly that.

pairs.q: what is the principle of least privilege
pairs.a: Give each component the smallest permissions it needs; MyGPT reads its data dir and writes only its own state.
A rate limiter where tokens refill steadily, each request spends one, and an empty bucket means wait.
Retrying with growing delays so a struggling server can recover — add jitter so clients don't retry in lockstep.
After repeated failures, stop calling a dependency for a while instead of piling on — fail fast, recover gently.
Logs, metrics and traces that make a running system understandable from outside — my /api/health and /api/analytics are small examples.
Bucketing observations to see distributions, not just averages — p95 latency explains user pain better than the mean.
A unique id per request letting logs across services be stitched into one story.
Finishing in-flight work, flushing state and closing connections when asked to stop — MyGPT flushes data on exit.
A versioned change moving stored data to the next schema so upgrades don't lose history.
Collecting the least data, storing it locally, making deletion easy — MyGPT keeps everything on your machine.
Starter knowledge a system boots with before it learns anything — seed_corpus.json in this project.

pairs.q: what is human in the loop
pairs.a: Keeping a person as the decision point: MyGPT asks you to teach it instead of pretending to know.

pairs.q: what is the ai alignment problem
pairs.a: Making increasingly capable systems reliably pursue intended goals; at this scale it means transparent, inspectable behaviour.
When a measure becomes a target it stops measuring well — a reason to keep several honest signals, not one number.
Shortcuts that speed today and slow tomorrow — track and repay them deliberately.
Improving structure without changing behaviour, with tests as the safety net.
A hint of deeper trouble: duplicated logic, giant functions, misleading names, comments explaining confusing code.
You Aren't Gonna Need It — build for the current requirement, cleanly, not for imagined futures.
Keep It Simple — the simplest thing that works is easiest to trust, test and change.
Don't Repeat Yourself — one authoritative implementation of each piece of knowledge.

pairs.q: what is the boy scout rule
pairs.a: Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it; small constant improvements beat big rewrites.
Explaining the bug aloud to an inanimate listener often reveals it before you finish the sentence.
The chain of calls leading to an exception — read from the bottom (outermost) to the top (where it broke).
A deliberate pause (breakpoint() or pdb) letting you inspect variables at the moment of interest.
Logs carry levels, timestamps and destinations; prints vanish in production. Use logging in anything that ships.
A claim the code guarantees true — for catching programmer errors in development, not for validating user input.
Validate early and loudly so problems surface near their cause instead of corrupting distant state.
Handing out copies of internal lists/dicts so callers can't mutate your state behind your back.
A runtime switch that enables or hides behaviour, letting you ship dark and turn things on safely.
Giving a new version a small slice of traffic first, watching, then widening.
Returning to the previous known-good version — fast rollback beats a perfect release process.
A blameless write-up after an incident: what happened, why, and what changes prevent a repeat.
An Architecture Decision Record: a short note capturing a decision, its context and consequences for future readers.
Clear sentences, short paragraphs, examples over adjectives. If a reader must re-read, rewrite.
A one-line need from the user's perspective: 'as a learner I want instant answers so I keep momentum'.
The smallest version delivering real value — seeded knowledge plus chat, before any extras existed.
Using your own product; every feature here was exercised in this chat interface before shipping.
Showing the simple face first and details on request — advanced panels hide behind tabs and collapsed traces.
A thin feature touching every layer (UI → API → brain → tests) instead of one layer across many features.
Firing one end-to-end example through the whole system early so every integration point is proven.
A chain of tasks enabled by other tasks. Name it, timebox it, return to the real goal.
A fixed budget for an attempt so exploration can't eat the schedule — finish, ship, iterate.
The checklist a change must pass: works, tested, documented, changelogged, no regressions.
Specific, testable conditions a change must satisfy — the basis of every test in this repo.
Driving realistic traffic to find the breaking point before your users do.
Deliberately breaking dependencies to verify graceful failure — my clients prove offline behaviour against dead ports.
400s blame the request (bad payload), 500s blame the server (a bug). Don't retry a 400 unchanged.
Too Many Requests — you hit a rate limit; back off and retry later, respecting Retry-After.
Service Unavailable — temporarily overloaded or under maintenance; retrying later is reasonable.
No Content — success with nothing to send; my CORS preflight answers this way.
Automatically retrying only safe methods (GET, PUT); never blind-retry a POST that may have succeeded.

pairs.q: what is a webhook versus polling
pairs.a: Webhooks push events to you, polling asks repeatedly — push wins when events are sparse and you own both ends.
Writes propagate asynchronously so readers may briefly see older data — fine when nothing needs instant agreement.

pairs.q: what is a write ahead log
pairs.a: Appending intent before applying it so a crash mid-write can be recovered — my append-only episode log follows the spirit.
Writing a temp file then renaming over the target so readers never see half-written data — every save here does this.
A short digest of data that detects corruption in transit or at rest.
A periodic 'still alive' signal; the header status dot is the human-facing version.
An interface that forces you to understand the layer beneath it — good abstractions keep secrets.

pairs.q: what is the law of demeter
pairs.a: Talk to your immediate collaborators, not their internals: obj.name beats obj.wrapper.inner.name.
Passing collaborators in instead of constructing them inside — the reason my tests can inject temp dirs and dead ports.
The framework calls you (callbacks, hooks) rather than you calling it — Flask routes work this way.
Same inputs produce the same outputs and effects — the property that makes testing and debugging tractable.
Anything beyond returning a value: writing files, bumping counters, sending requests. Name them, isolate them, test them.
Refusing nonsense early with a clear 400 instead of crashing deep inside a pipeline.

pairs.q: what is a data retention policy
pairs.a: How long data lives and what deletes it; my episodes cap at 2000 and you can clear the transcript any time.
Slowing producers when consumers can't keep up — the skill queue drains gently instead of spawning unbounded work.
A counter limiting how many threads hold a resource at once — use it where a plain lock over-restricts.
Two parties each holding what the other waits for. Avoid by locking in a fixed order or not nesting locks.
Randomising retry delays so many clients don't retry in lockstep and re-crush a recovering server.
A clock that never goes backwards (time.monotonic) — correct for measuring durations, unlike wall-clock time.

pairs.q: what is utc versus local time
pairs.a: Store UTC, display local; every timestamp in my data files is UTC epoch seconds.
Seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC — compact, sortable and unambiguous.
The yyyy-mm-dd form that sorts correctly as text and is unambiguous across locales.
One agreed representation of a value (lowercased, trimmed, punctuation-stripped) so lookups succeed — my normalize().
Chopping suffixes so 'running' and 'run' match: my content tokens strip simple plural/ing endings.
Dropping very common words that carry little retrieval signal — I weight them near zero instead of deleting them.
The document ids attached to each term in an inverted index.
How often a term appears in a document — one half of tf-idf.
How many documents contain a term; rare terms are more informative, hence the inverse weighting.
The sum of element-wise products; with normalisation it gives cosine similarity, the core of my retrieval.
Doing maths on whole arrays in C instead of Python loops — the difference between milliseconds and seconds here.
NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes without explicitly copying data.

pairs.q: what is a view versus a copy
pairs.a: A view shares memory (fast, risky), a copy is independent (safe, costs memory); slicing usually views.
The code run most often; it deserves the clearest naming and the most care about allocations.
The one component limiting overall speed — fixing anything else changes nothing.
The first, slower run before caches warm up — visible in the ⏱ latency tags on each reply.
Reusing prepared data so the next call is fast — my probe TTLs and tokenizer cache are small examples.
Roughly 80% of the effect comes from 20% of the causes; find that 20% before optimising anything else.
An object usable as a dict key must not change its hash — lists can't, tuples of immutables can.
Two different keys landing in one bucket; dicts resolve them, but adversarial collisions can degrade performance.
The occupancy ratio that triggers a hash table to resize — Python resizes around two-thirds full.
A tree rebalanced (red-black, AVL) to keep its height logarithmic so lookups stay predictable.
A wide, shallow tree used by databases and filesystems so one disk read fetches many keys.
A structure tracking which elements are connected (Disjoint Set Union) with near-constant-time operations.
Ordering a DAG so every edge points forward — how build tools decide what compiles first.
The classic shortest-path algorithm for non-negative weights, always extending the closest known frontier.
A* — Dijkstra guided by a heuristic estimating remaining distance, the basis of game pathfinding.

pairs.q: what is a minimum spanning tree
pairs.a: The cheapest edge set connecting every node; Kruskal and Prim build it.
A structure answering range queries and point updates in logarithmic time.
All suffixes of a string sorted, letting substring search run in logarithmic time.
A hash updatable in constant time as a window slides — the trick behind fast substring search.
Knuth-Morris-Pratt: a failure table so a mismatch never re-scans already-matched characters.

pairs.q: what is meet in the middle
pairs.a: Splitting an exponential search in two halves and joining results, turning 2ⁿ into 2^(n/2).
A system whose behaviour depends on current state plus input; skills, backends and circuit breakers are small ones.
The formal model behind regexes and state machines: states, transitions, accept states.
No program can decide for every program whether it terminates — the reason static analysis must approximate.
Can every quickly-checkable problem also be quickly solvable? Nobody knows; a million dollars waits.
The hardest problems in NP — solve one quickly and you solve them all: SAT, timetabling, travelling salesman.

pairs.q: what is the travelling salesman problem
pairs.a: Visit every city once, minimise distance: exact for small n, heuristics beyond.
n+1 items in n holes forces a collision — the basis of hash inevitability and many counting proofs.
Something true at every step (loop invariants prove correctness) or across a system (my counters only grow on teach).
Prove a base case and an inductive step, and all cases follow — the standard way to reason about recursion.
A single case that breaks a claim; searching for one is faster than arguing.
Among equally good explanations, prefer the simplest — one more reason this codebase avoids dependencies.
Work expands to fill the time available — hence deliberately small release scopes.
Systems mirror the communication structure of the teams that built them.

pairs.q: what is the map is not the territory
pairs.a: Models are simplifications; my retrieval scores approximate relevance, they don't capture meaning.

pairs.q: what is symbolic versus statistical ai
pairs.a: Rules and logic versus learned probabilities — MyGPT is deliberately both, with templates and memory on one side and a tiny neural LM on the other.
Being able to say why an answer appeared: my chain-of-thought traces, mode tags and retrieval scores exist for that.
A number expressing certainty; a template match is 0.85, a wild guess 0.3 — and I show it.
Whether stated confidence matches reality; overconfident systems are worse than silent ones, hence honest fallbacks.
Fluent text unmoored from truth. Mitigations here: retrieval, templates, low-confidence phrasing, and refusing to pretend.
A hard limit preventing a bad class of action — no code execution, no file writing, strict size caps.
Make correcting the system easy (👍/👎, inline corrections) and actually use the signal (reinforcement, retraining).
Raising the weight of answers that worked so they surface sooner — my 👍 directly changes ranking.
Learning new things badly enough to lose old ones — why training rounds here mix in the core corpus.
Rehearsing stored examples alongside new ones to retain old knowledge.
Learning from the data's own structure (predict the next token) without human labels — my tiny LM's whole regime.

pairs.q: what is a knowledge base versus a model
pairs.a: A knowledge base stores explicit facts you can inspect and delete; a model stores implicit statistics. MyGPT keeps both.
Where a fact came from — seed corpus, your teaching, or an import; my stores tag each.
A marker recording a deletion so it can propagate — my forget path removes the pair and logs the event.
Teaching the same question twice replaces the old answer instead of duplicating — memory.add(replace_question=...).
Removing identical or near-identical items; the seed corpus is verified duplicate-free by a test.
Automated checks that must pass before shipping: tests, compile, JSON validity and a live smoke test.
Verifying prerequisites before heavy work — the browser's OPTIONS preflight, or checking the venv before starting servers.
One place to see service health; /api/health reports version, uptime and dependency reachability.
Who might attack what, and how: for a localhost app the main risks are malformed input and path traversal — both covered by tests.
Naming a file like ../../etc/passwd to escape a directory; my checkpoint endpoints reject it and a test proves it.
Feeding random or hostile inputs to find crashes — my validation tests cover empties, huge payloads and wrong types.
Escaping data when rendering so it can't become code — chat text uses textContent, never innerHTML.
All-or-nothing updates; a temp-file-plus-rename write is atomic at the file level.
Surviving a crash after acknowledging a write — save(force=True) on user-critical actions, flush on exit.

pairs.q: what is a single writer principle
pairs.a: One component owns each piece of state, making races impossible — the Flask lock serialises brain mutations.
A queue with a maximum length that applies backpressure instead of growing forever.

pairs.q: what is an unbounded growth bug
pairs.a: A list that only ever grows — the cause of most long-running leaks; every store here has a cap.
A component that revives something stuck; my background trainer tolerates a stalled worker without blocking chat.
Trying the real operation cheaply to learn whether it's available — my backend probes hit /health instead of assuming.
Settings stated in one place (env vars here) rather than magic numbers scattered through code.

pairs.q: what is a twelve factor app
pairs.a: Config in the environment, stateless processes, logs as streams, dev/prod parity — the checklist this app broadly follows.
One deployable process holding the whole system; for a personal chatbot that's the correct, simplest choice.
How much one module must know about another; loose coupling is why the brain is testable without Flask.
How tightly a module's parts belong together — high cohesion inside memory.py, low coupling outward.
A stand-in for a real dependency (fake, stub, spy) — my dead-port clients are the simplest kind.
One that passes offline, anywhere, deterministically — every test here is hermetic by construction.
A quick check the build isn't on fire: page loads, health is green, one chat round-trips.
Each test builds and tears down its own world so ordering never matters — every suite here gets a temp dir and a fresh brain.
Stored expected output compared every run; ideal for API shapes and exports.
A test that passes and fails without code changes — usually timing or shared state. Fix the cause, never retry-loop it.
Designing so everyone can use it: keyboard paths, screen-reader labels, contrast, reduced motion, scalable text.
Accessible Rich Internet Applications: attributes like aria-label and aria-live that describe UI to assistive tech.
The luminance difference between text and background; WCAG AA wants at least 4.5:1 for body text.
A user preference (prefers-reduced-motion) asking for fewer animations; honouring it prevents discomfort.
Using button, nav, main and label for what they mean rather than divs with handlers — free keyboard support.
The label a control is announced with — visible text, aria-label, or a linked <label> element.
The sequence Tab moves focus through; it should follow reading order and stay away from positive tabindex values.
A first-focus 'skip to content' link letting keyboard users bypass repeated navigation.
Designing so text, dates and numbers adapt to other locales — toLocaleTimeString handles my dates.

pairs.q: what is a time zone bug
pairs.a: Storing local times instead of UTC, then adding offsets twice. Store UTC, convert at the display edge.
A font where every glyph shares one width, so code columns line up.
Adding a web app to the desktop/home screen via its manifest; it opens without browser chrome.
Designing so the app still works without a network — queue actions, serve cached data, sync later.
A small browser key-value store, ideal for drafts and preferences but unsuitable for large or sensitive data.
A background script between page and network enabling offline caching and push — the engine behind PWAs.
Waiting for quiet before acting — the memory search fires 220 ms after you stop typing.
Showing the user's action immediately, then reconciling with the server — why chat feels instant.
A short-lived corner message confirming an action; I use them for copies, clears, themes and imports.
Bigger, closer targets are faster to hit — why the send button is large and pinned beside the composer.
More choices take longer to decide — hence Auto mode and a short model list instead of a wall of options.
A named value (colour, radius, spacing) reused everywhere; my CSS variables made the light theme one block of code.
Flex is one-dimensional flow, grid is two-dimensional placement; this layout uses flex, with grid for tile rows.
How fast something feels — instant composer feedback, typing dots and streamed words all shorten the felt wait.

pairs.q: what is cpu versus io bound
pairs.a: CPU-bound work is limited by computation (use processes); I/O-bound work waits on network or disk (threads or async).
Timing one tiny operation — easily misleading; measure whole operations instead.
A server fronting your app for TLS, compression and headers — I run a tiny one in front of the Cortex dashboard.
Reusing one TCP connection for several requests, cutting handshake cost — my Cortex and Ollama clients do this.
A response fingerprint browsers send back to skip unchanged downloads.
Working acceptably when features are missing — no clipboard access still explains what to do.
Start with working HTML, then layer JavaScript niceties so the base never breaks.
Trying options in order until one works: streaming → plain chat, Cortex → Ollama → brain, clipboard → toast.
Least-Recently-Used eviction: when full, discard the entry unused longest — functools.lru_cache implements it.
Time to live — how long a cached answer stays valid; my backend probes reuse results for 20 seconds.
A description of allowed structure; validating chat payloads (text, non-empty, ≤4000) is a tiny schema.
A test verifying client and server agree on the interface — my tests pin the exact JSON of every endpoint.
Past bug fixes accumulated as permanent tests — every bug fixed in this project gained one.
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few slow end-to-end ones — cheap feedback dominates.
A prefix tree storing strings by their characters — it powers autocomplete like my /api/suggest.
A tiny probabilistic set that answers 'definitely not present' or 'maybe present', with no false negatives.
Term frequency × inverse document frequency: favours words common in one document but rare overall. My retrieval weights this way.
A map from word to the documents containing it, so search visits candidates instead of scanning everything.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors — 1 identical, 0 unrelated. It's how questions match memories here.

pairs.q: what is edit distance used for
pairs.a: Spelling correction, fuzzy matching and diffing — the fewest single-character edits between two strings.
The classic edit distance: insertions, deletions and substitutions, each costing one.

pairs.q: what is a monte carlo method
pairs.a: Estimating an answer by random sampling — like simulating dice rolls to see the distribution.
With just 23 people a shared birthday is more likely than not — intuition about probability is bad.

pairs.q: what is the law of large numbers
pairs.a: Averages converge to the true mean as samples grow — why more dice rolls give flatter bars.
The bell curve: most values near the mean with thinning tails, described by mean and standard deviation.
The typical distance of values from their mean — the square root of variance.

pairs.q: what is a median versus mean
pairs.a: The median splits sorted data in half and ignores outliers; the mean can be dragged by them. Report both when data is skewed.
The value below which a given share of data falls — p95 latency is the 95th percentile of response times.
Correlation means two things move together; causation means one drives the other. Ice cream sales and drownings correlate — summer causes both.
The probability of seeing data at least this extreme if nothing were happening — small suggests a real effect, not proof.
Updating beliefs with evidence: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. It answers 'how likely is this cause, given what I saw?'
How common something is overall; ignoring it causes alarms at rare events that fit common patterns.
A series of if/else splits partitioning data — readable, and the ancestor of random forests.
Classify a point by the votes of its nearest examples — simple, effective, with no training step.
Clustering by iterating: assign points to the nearest of k centres, move each centre to its cluster's mean, repeat.
Predicting a number rather than a category; linear regression fits the best straight line.
The non-linearity between layers (relu, tanh, softmax) that lets networks model curved relationships.
Turns a vector of scores into probabilities summing to one — used for the next-token distribution.
How big a step gradient descent takes — too large bounces or diverges, too small crawls.
How many examples gradients are averaged over before a step; bigger batches are smoother but need more memory.
One full pass over the training data; the Train button here uses 5–50 epochs.
Randomly ignoring neurons during training to prevent co-adaptation and overfitting.
When training accidentally sees test information — evaluation looks great, reality doesn't.
Turning raw data into informative inputs: ratios, flags, counts, n-grams.
Removing one component at a time to see whether it actually helps — the honest way to justify complexity.
The simplest reasonable result to beat; improvement without a baseline is meaningless.
Same code, same data, same seed → same result. Seeds, pinned dependencies and recorded configs get you there.
The starting point for a pseudo-random sequence; fixing it makes runs repeatable — my tiny LM is seeded.
A standard task for comparing approaches — and a reminder to measure before optimising.
Making code complicated for speed before knowing it matters. Profile first.
Measuring where time actually goes — cProfile, py-spy and time.perf_counter are the usual tools.
Computing only when needed — generators, itertools and short-circuit boolean logic all illustrate it.
and/or stop as soon as the answer is known; guard clauses like 'if user and user.active' rely on it.
Same inputs → same output, no side effects. Trivial to test and safe to cache.
Each module does one job — tokenizer, memory, brain, codegen and clients here are separate and independently testable.

pairs.q: what is a proof by contradiction
pairs.a: Assume the opposite and derive impossibility — how the irrationality of √2 is shown.

pairs.q: what is a necessary versus sufficient condition
pairs.a: Necessary must hold (fuel to drive); sufficient guarantees it (full tank and a working car).
A tool to pause execution, inspect variables and step through code — pdb is Python's built-in one.
Reading someone's change for bugs, clarity and fit before merging — not gatekeeping style a formatter handles.
A proposal to merge a branch, carrying the diff, the discussion and the checks.
A named pointer to the exact commit that shipped, like v1.9.0 — my changelog numbers map onto these.
Old clients keep working: add fields, don't rename or remove them, unless a major version says otherwise.
Announcing that something will be removed, keeping it working for a while, documenting the replacement.
The written promise about inputs, outputs, errors and status codes; the README table is its public face.
Step-by-step recovery instructions for common failures, written while calm for use while not.
How much breaks when something fails; small isolated components keep it small.

pairs.q: what is the principle of least astonishment
pairs.a: Interfaces should behave the way people expect — Enter sends, Escape clears, nothing surprising.
Retrieving an answer without looking beats re-reading — try asking me before searching.
Explain it simply; wherever you stumble is where you don't yet understand it.
Working at the edge of ability with feedback on specific weaknesses — the reason tests and latency tags exist.
Focused uninterrupted effort on demanding tasks; the reason this UI is quiet by default.
Shipping a thin slice end-to-end rather than half of six features.

pairs.q: what is a non functional requirement
pairs.a: Qualities like speed, portability and accessibility that no feature list captures but users feel immediately.

pairs.q: what is a graceful error message
pairs.a: One sentence saying what happened and what to do next, without a stack trace and without blaming the user.
One request triggering many downstream calls — powerful, but latency and failure multiply.
A scheduled command; my brain runs its own gentle background cycle instead of relying on system cron.
Starting twice changes nothing harmful — directories are created with exist_ok and state loads if present.
A stored number saying which schema a file uses so future code can migrate instead of guessing.
A sensible value used when configuration is missing: port 8000, cortex url localhost, plain Brain if nothing answers.

pairs.q: what is a denial of service
pairs.a: Overwhelming a service with volume; caps on message size, batch size and body length are the first defence.
Running out of memory, handles or disk — bounded queues, capped logs and streamed reads keep it away.
A short throwaway experiment answering one question; delete it afterwards, keep the knowledge.

pairs.q: what is a proof of concept
pairs.a: The smallest build showing the idea is possible — like the first version of this chat.
Keeping every commit releasable via automation; continuous deployment goes further and ships automatically.
Describing servers in versioned files rather than hand-typed commands, so environments reproduce.
A packaged process with its dependencies isolated from the host — Docker is the common tool.
Mapping a host port to a service inside an isolated network — how the sandbox preview reaches my 0.0.0.0:8000.
Shrinking responses before sending, typically 70%+ smaller for text at a small CPU cost.

pairs.q: what is a cache busting query
pairs.a: Appending a version to a file URL so browsers fetch the new copy after a deploy.
Deferring work until needed — images, panels and heavy modules loaded only when they come into view.
A placeholder outline while content loads, reducing the felt wait versus a blank panel.
Users should reach any feature within about three interactions; tabs, chips and shortcuts keep me inside that budget.
A font loaded by the page; I use system fonts instead — zero network cost and no layout shift.
How much RAM a process uses; the small LM plus a 2000-episode cap keeps MyGPT modest on a laptop.
Non-perishable things last longer the longer they've already lasted — a guide for what to bet on.
